title: Why is the world green?
teaches: How a predator can protect plants it never eats, and why food chains flip in alternation

blocks.text: Look out over almost any stretch of land that people leave alone, and most of what you see is plants. Every leaf is food for something: caterpillars, aphids, grasshoppers, deer, rabbits, voles, slugs. There are millions of kinds of plant-eater, many of them able to multiply as fast as lesson 2's flies. So why haven't they eaten it all? Why is the world still green?

In 1960 three ecologists at the University of Michigan, Nelson Hairston, Frederick Smith and Lawrence Slobodkin, published a four-page answer that ecologists still argue about.[^hss] Plant-eaters, they said, are rarely short of food: the leaves are there, uneaten. So something else must be holding them down, and the obvious candidates are their own predators and diseases. Plants are left to compete with each other for light, water and soil. Predators, at the top, are limited by how much prey they can catch.

The striking part is the first step. If they were right, a hawk or a wolf or a ladybird protects plants it never touches, by eating the animals that would eat them. An effect jumps a level. But a four-page argument from looking around is not a test. The test came from a cold sea, fourteen years later.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin (1960): plant-eaters are held down by their predators, so plants survive.
If so, a predator protects plants it never eats.

blocks.text: Sea otters once lived along the whole North Pacific rim, from Japan to the Aleutian Islands to Baja California. Their fur is the densest of any animal,[^otter-fur] and from the 1740s fur traders hunted them almost to extinction. By 1911, when a treaty stopped the hunt, a few small colonies were left. One was at Amchitka, in the western Aleutians. By the 1970s otters there were back to full numbers. On Shemya, an island about 350 kilometres west, there were still none.

In 1971 a young graduate student, James Estes, went diving at both. At Amchitka the shallow sea floor was covered in a forest of kelp, big brown seaweed reaching up to the surface, full of fish. The sea urchins there were few and small and stayed in cracks. At Shemya the urchins were large and so crowded that they covered the rock, and there was almost no kelp at all: a bare floor ecologists call an **urchin barren**.

blocks.caption: Two Aleutian islands as Estes and Palmisano described them in 1974: with sea otters, a kelp forest; without, an urchin barren.

blocks.text: The link is food. A sea otter has no blubber, and keeps warm by burning food, eating about a quarter of its own weight every day. Urchins are one of its main prey. Where otters live, urchins are eaten faster than they can grow up, and those that survive hide. Urchins eat kelp, gnawing through the stalks where it holds on to the rock. Without otters, urchins multiply and graze every holdfast, and the forest goes. Estes and his colleague John Palmisano published the comparison in 1974: the otter, by eating urchins, keeps the kelp forest standing.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Amchitka had sea otters and a kelp forest; Shemya had no otters, crowds of urchins and almost no kelp.
Otters eat urchins; urchins eat kelp. By eating urchins, otters protect the kelp.

blocks.text: Effects that pass down a food chain from the top, skipping a level each time, are called a **trophic cascade**, from the Greek *trophē*, food. Robert Paine, of the sea star experiment, coined the phrase in 1980. A cascade follows from the stock-and-flow thinking of lessons 2 to 4. Each level is a stock that the level above drains. Hold a level down and you take the pressure off the one below it, which grows, which presses harder on the one below that.

blocks.caption: A food chain of one to four levels at its balance. Kelp grows up to the room it has; each level eats the one below it. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then add orcas to the chain of three

blocks.text: Count the levels and a pattern appears. With one level, the kelp fills its room. With two, the grazers eat it down. With three, the predators hold the grazers down and the plants come back. With four, the top predators hold the middle predators down, the grazers come back, and the plants are eaten again. Chains with an odd number of levels end in plenty of plants; chains with an even number end in bare ground. That is the simple model; real webs, as the next sections show, are messier.

Try the hunting slider too. Make the top level hunt harder and the level just below it falls, the one below that rises, and so on down, in alternation. In the model the top level itself barely gains: a better hunter mostly thins its own prey.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A **trophic cascade** is an effect that passes down a food chain, flipping at each level.
Odd numbers of levels end in plenty of plants; even numbers end in few.

blocks.text: The Aleutians ran the four-level experiment by themselves. Through the 1990s Estes and his colleagues, still counting otters along the islands, watched their numbers fall by roughly 90 percent across hundreds of kilometres of coast. The otters weren't starving or sick, and there were no bodies on the beaches. Then they began to see orcas, killer whales, hunting them. Orcas had always shared the coast with otters but had rarely bothered with something so small and bony.[^orca-math]

In 1998 the team showed what followed. Where otters had gone, urchins multiplied and the kelp forests thinned and turned to barrens again. In one sheltered lagoon on Adak, which orcas couldn't easily enter, the otters held on and so did the kelp. Why the orcas changed their diet is still argued about; one idea is that the seals and sea lions they usually eat had declined, perhaps a long echo of the great whales taken by whaling. But the chain had gained a fourth level, and the kelp went, just as the arithmetic says.

Washington has its own otter story. The last of the state's sea otters were shot in the early 1900s. In 1969 and 1970, 59 otters from Amchitka were flown to the outer coast, and their descendants now number in the thousands, from Destruction Island to Neah Bay. Divers there have watched kelp return to rocks the urchins had stripped.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: In the 1990s orcas began eating Aleutian sea otters; otters fell about 90 percent, urchins rose, and the kelp went.
Adding a fourth level to the chain flipped the plants back to few.

blocks.text: On land the most famous cascade story is Yellowstone. Wolves were exterminated from the park by the 1920s. Elk multiplied, browsed the willows and aspens along the streams, and over decades the willows shrank to stubs. In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves were brought down from Canada and released. Within a few years some streamside willows were growing tall again, and the story was told everywhere: wolves came back, elk were eaten or scared off the streams, willows grew, and songbirds and beavers returned.

The full story turned out to be more tangled. Elk numbers fell for several reasons at once, including hunting outside the park, bears, and hard winters. And the willows recovered in some places but not others. In 2013 Kristin Marshall, Tom Hobbs and David Cooper reported an experiment along four Yellowstone streams. They fenced some willows to keep elk off, and built small dams beside some of them to raise the water as beaver dams once had. After ten years, the willows grew tallest only where both had been done: no elk *and* high water.

Without beavers, the streams had cut down into their beds and the water table had dropped below the willows' roots. Taking the elk away wasn't enough on its own; the land had changed while the wolves were gone. A cascade can run down a chain, but switching the top back on doesn't always run it back up.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Yellowstone's wolves helped some willows recover, but elk also fell for other reasons.
Willows grew tallest only where elk were kept off *and* the water table was raised, as beavers once did.
Restoring a top predator doesn't always undo the cascade its loss caused.

parts.title: The other answer: plants fight back

blocks.text: Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin's paper drew an immediate reply. Plants, critics pointed out, are not simply sitting there waiting to be eaten. Most leaves are tough, hairy, spiny, low in protein, or laced with poisons. A caterpillar surrounded by green may be surrounded by things it can't digest. As the ecologistJohn Lawton later put it, the world is prickly and tastes bad.

Both answers are right somewhere. Kelp is soft and nutritious, and on kelp coasts predators decide what stays. On land, much of the green is protected by the plants themselves, and plant-eaters spend their lives picking out the few parts they can use. The Botany course comes back to this: tannins, nicotine, and the chemical war between plants and insects.

What lasted from the argument is the shape of the question. To understand why something is abundant, look at what it eats, what eats it, and what eats that. Effects reach across levels, and a species you never see may be the reason a place looks the way it does.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The rival answer: the world is green because much of it is tough or poisonous.
Both hold somewhere: soft kelp is protected by predators; much land vegetation protects itself.

blocks.caption: Six questions on cascades
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A lake has algae, water fleas that eat algae, and small fish that eat water fleas. Pike are added, and they eat the small fish. What happens to the algae?
choices: No change: pike don't eat algae
items.why: Four levels now. Pike thin the small fish, so water fleas multiply and graze the algae down. The lake gets clearer.

items.ask: Why was there almost no kelp at Shemya in 1971?
choices: With no otters to eat them, urchins grazed it away
The water was too cold for kelp
items.why: Otters eat urchins, not kelp. Without otters, urchins multiplied and ate the kelp down to bare rock.

items.ask: A food chain has three levels: grass, rabbits, foxes. Foxes start hunting harder. What happens to the grass?
items.why: Harder hunting thins the rabbits, which takes pressure off the grass. Effects flip at each level.

items.ask: What did Marshall, Hobbs and Cooper find about Yellowstone's willows?
choices: They grew tallest only where elk were kept off and the water table was raised
They recovered everywhere once wolves returned
items.why: Without beavers the streams had cut down and the water table had dropped. Willows needed both protection from elk and high water.

items.ask: Which observation supports the 'plants fight back' answer to why the world is green?
choices: Caterpillars surrounded by leaves still go hungry because most leaves are poisonous to them
items.why: If much of the green is inedible, plant-eaters can be scarce even without predators. That is the rival answer to Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin.

items.ask: In the 1990s orcas began eating sea otters in the Aleutians. Which level of the chain ended up with more?
items.why: Orcas thinned the otters, which freed the urchins from their main predator. More urchins then ate down the kelp.

summary: **Why haven't plant-eaters eaten everything?** Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin (1960) answered: their predators hold them down.
**Otters protect kelp.** At Amchitka otters ate urchins and kelp forests stood; at Shemya, with no otters, urchins left bare rock (Estes and Palmisano, 1974).
**A trophic cascade passes down a chain, flipping at each level.** Chains with three levels end with plenty of plants; with two or four, few.
**The Aleutians added a fourth level.** When orcas began eating otters in the 1990s, urchins rose and the kelp went.
**Yellowstone's willows needed more than wolves.** They grew tallest only where elk were kept off and beaver-high water came back.
**Plants also fight back.** Much of the world is green because it is tough or poisonous.
**Look two levels up.** A species you never see can be why a place looks as it does.

hss.title: HSS
hss.text: Ecologists still call the argument 'HSS', from the three authors' initials. Their paper in *The American Naturalist* was titled 'Community Structure, Population Control, and Competition' and had no data tables or equations, only four pages of plain reasoning.

otter-fur.title: Sea otter fur
otter-fur.text: A sea otter has up to 150,000 hairs per square centimetre, more than on an entire human head. The coat traps a layer of air against the skin so water never touches it, as long as the fur stays clean.

orca-math.title: Four orcas would do it
orca-math.text: Estes and his colleagues calculated how many killer whales it would take to eat 40,000 sea otters in six years. An adult orca needs so many calories that a single whale living exclusively on otters would eat about 1,800 of them a year. Fewer than four orcas could have caused the entire collapse.
